strengths: FixAgent presents a coherent, training-free debugging pipeline combining localization, repair, review, and explicit variable tracking. Allowing repairs beyond initially localized statements addresses a practical limitation of rigid localization–repair pipelines. The work is relevant to NLP research on language-model reasoning and code.

The reported repair gains are substantial: 2,701 plausible Codeflaws repairs versus GPT-4’s 2,115, and 79/80 correct QuixBugs repairs versus 74/80 for GPT-4. These results provide promising evidence of practical utility.

Experiments cover three programming languages and several base models. Table III reports improvements across all five evaluated models, while the ablations provide useful evidence that program context and variable-tracking instructions contribute beyond generic chain-of-thought prompting.

The manuscript distinguishes plausible from correct patches, performs manual correctness checks, specifies model versions and sampling settings, and reports releasing code and generated patches. These are useful foundations for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The test-oracle protocol is insufficiently specified. The crafter requires externally computed expected outputs, but the experiments do not identify the checker, oracle source, generated-test budget, or which tests each baseline receives. How generated tests enter repair feedback versus final assessment is also unclear. These details are essential for assessing automation, comparison fairness, and overfitting; the crafter has no dedicated ablation.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate benefits from agent specialization versus additional inference. Three patch attempts do not equalize model calls or generated tokens across a multi-agent pipeline and a single-model baseline. A comparable-budget iterative debugging baseline is needed. Closely related approaches already cited, including self-debugging [70] and conversational repair [28], are discussed but not experimentally compared.

The headline 97.26% correctness rate is not transparently reconciled with the reported results. In Table I, FixAgent and GPT-4 both obtain 93 correct patches among 100 audited Codeflaws patches, which supports increased repair yield but does not establish improved conditional correctness. Sampling is reasonable, but uncertainty intervals and a clearer manual-adjudication protocol are needed before drawing strong conclusions about overcoming overfitting.

The contamination argument is too strong. A dataset’s collection date and low GitHub popularity do not establish that its underlying problems and solutions were absent from each model’s training data. Moreover, Table II reports only FixAgent variants on ConDefects, without corresponding base-model results. Consequently, the newer dataset does not establish the claimed improvement over base models under reduced contamination risk.

The subsets supporting the ablations need better characterization. GPT-4’s plausible-repair rate is 75.7% on the 300-bug Codeflaws subset, compared with 54.2% on the full dataset; FixAgent’s rates also differ substantially. This does not demonstrate biased selection, but requires explaining the sampling procedure and releasing sample identifiers. Repeated-run or paired uncertainty analysis would also strengthen conclusions from stochastic generation.

The broader claims exceed the demonstrated scope. Contest programs and classic algorithms provide limited evidence for repository dependency handling, complex production debugging, or explanation usefulness. The claimed first application of rubber ducking also needs clearer differentiation from the acknowledged self-debugging work [70]. These contribution limits weaken the main-conference case; the unresolved evaluation and reproducibility issues above keep the recommendation at borderline Findings.
